title: What are the three forms of JPA projections (interface-based, class/DTO constructor, dynamic generic), how does each work, and when do you use which?
shortTitle: Interface, class/DTO constructor, dynamic generic projections?

s1_definition.profdef: A JPA projection returns only the columns an application actually needs instead of the whole entity. Spring Data supports three forms. The first is the INTERFACE projection: you declare a plain Java interface with getter methods (`getFdId()`, `getMaturityAmount()`), Spring Data builds a proxy at runtime that is backed by only those columns. The second is the CLASS/DTO projection: you either write a JPQL constructor expression `SELECT new com.bank.dto.FdSummary(f.fdId, f.maturityAmount) FROM FixedDeposit f`, or let Spring Data map directly into a `record`. The third is the DYNAMIC projection: a single repository method declared with a generic type parameter `<T> List<T> findByAccountId(String accountId, Class<T> type)` where the caller passes the projection class at runtime, so the same query can return a lightweight interface, a DTO, or the full entity on demand.
s1_definition.analogy: Rajesh asks National Bank of India for his fixed-deposit details. The interface projection is a clerk who photocopies only the two lines you asked for onto a slip. The DTO projection is a clerk who hands you a pre-printed receipt with exactly those fields already laid out. The dynamic projection is a clerk who asks "which format would you like today?" and prints whichever one you name at the counter.
s1_definition.oneliner: Interface projection is a proxy over selected getters, DTO/class projection is a `new` constructor expression or record (fastest and most explicit), and dynamic projection takes a `Class<T>` parameter so the caller chooses the shape at runtime.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A JPA projection returns only the columns an application actually needs instead of the whole entity. Spring Data supports three forms. The first is the INTERFACE projection: you declare a plain Java interface with getter methods (`getFdId()`, `getMaturityAmount()`), Spring Data builds a proxy at runtime that is backed by only those columns. The second is the CLASS/DTO projection: you either write a JPQL constructor expression `SELECT new com.bank.dto.FdSummary(f.fdId, f.maturityAmount) FROM FixedDeposit f`, or let Spring Data map directly into a `record`. The third is the DYNAMIC projection: a single repository method declared with a generic type parameter `<T> List<T> findByAccountId(String accountId, Class<T> type)` where the caller passes the projection class at runtime, so the same query can return a lightweight interface, a DTO, or the full entity on demand.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Rajesh asks National Bank of India for his fixed-deposit details. The interface projection is a clerk who photocopies only the two lines you asked for onto a slip. The DTO projection is a clerk who hands you a pre-printed receipt with exactly those fields already laid out. The dynamic projection is a clerk who asks "which format would you like today?" and prints whichever one you name at the counter.

**One line to remember:** Interface projection is a proxy over selected getters, DTO/class projection is a `new` constructor expression or record (fastest and most explicit), and dynamic projection takes a `Class<T>` parameter so the caller chooses the shape at runtime.

sections.s3_banking:
Let me set the scene with a real problem from National Bank of India. Our fixed-deposit portal has three screens that all read the same `fixed_deposits` table, and we kept serving them all by loading full entities. That was wasteful and, in one case, dangerous.

Problem 1 — the summary list screen was loading everything. The screen that lists Rajesh's deposits only shows the deposit id and the maturity amount, yet we were loading all twelve columns including the audit fields, and every row entered the persistence context with a dirty-check snapshot. This is exactly where a closed interface projection helps: we declare an interface with just `getFdId()` and `getMaturityAmount()`, and Hibernate fetches only those two columns.

Problem 2 — the API response screen needed a clean, serialisable shape. The detail API returns id, principal, and maturity amount as JSON. Returning the entity risked lazy-proxy serialization issues and leaked internal fields. This is exactly where a DTO constructor projection helps: `SELECT new FdDto(...)` builds a plain record with precisely the three fields the API contract promises, with no proxies to trip over.

Problem 3 — the search screen needed two detail levels from one query. Depending on a toggle, the search either shows a compact row or a full drill-down. We did not want two near-identical finders. This is exactly where a dynamic projection helps: one `<T> findByAccountId(accountId, Class<T>)` method serves the compact interface, the DTO, or the full entity based on what the controller asks for.

Here is what the mini-project code will do. There is a `FixedDeposit` entity with twelve columns. There is a closed interface `FdSummary` exposing two getters. There is a `FdDto` record for the API. The `FixedDepositRepository` declares a closed interface finder, a JPQL constructor-expression finder returning `FdDto`, and a dynamic `<T>` finder. The `FdProjectionService` exposes three read methods, each annotated `@Transactional(readOnly = true)`, that call the three repository styles and log the column count for each. The `FdProjectionController` exposes the three endpoints. A test verifies the DTO record carries only the chosen fields and that the dynamic method can return different shapes.

```bash
# FORM 1 — interface projection (2 columns)

# SQL: SELECT f.fd_id, f.maturity_amount FROM fixed_deposits f WHERE f.account_id = 'SAV2001'

# FORM 2 — DTO constructor projection (3 columns)
curl "http://localhost:8360/api/v1/fd-projections/dto?status=ACTIVE"
# SQL: SELECT f.fd_id, f.principal, f.maturity_amount FROM fixed_deposits f WHERE f.status = 'ACTIVE'

# FORM 3 — dynamic projection (caller chose FdDto)
curl http://localhost:8360/api/v1/fd-projections/dynamic/SAV2001

# Run tests
mvn test
```
sections.s5_journey:
The input is a request to list Rajesh's fixed deposits for account `SAV2001`, followed by the API detail call and the dynamic search.

Step 1: The summary call enters `FdProjectionService.summaryByAccount("SAV2001")`, a `@Transactional(readOnly = true)` method, so a read-only Hibernate session is open and no dirty-check snapshots will be taken.

Step 2: The repository returns `List<FdSummary>`. Because `FdSummary` is a closed interface projection, Spring Data narrows the SQL to `SELECT f.fd_id, f.maturity_amount FROM fixed_deposits f WHERE f.account_id = 'SAV2001'`. Only two columns leave the database; the other ten columns including the large `notes` text are never read.

Step 3: Spring Data wraps each row in a lightweight proxy implementing `FdSummary`. These proxies do not enter the persistence context, so there is no snapshot and no dirty checking. The data for `fdId` and `maturityAmount` sits in the proxy; everything else about the row stays in the database.

Step 4: The DTO call runs `findDtoByStatus("ACTIVE")`. The JPQL constructor expression makes Hibernate run `new FdDto(fdId, principal, maturityAmount)` for each row, producing plain records. Three columns are fetched; the records are immutable value objects, safe to serialize to JSON after the session closes.

Step 5: The dynamic call runs `findByAccountId("SAV2001", FdDto.class)`. Spring Data inspects the passed class, sees it is not an entity, and materialises `FdDto` records using the same narrowing it would for a declared DTO finder. Had the caller passed `FixedDeposit.class`, the same method would have returned full managed entities instead.

```
2026-10-24 00:31:10 INFO  FdProjectionService - [INTERFACE] 2 rows, 2 columns (fd_id, maturity_amount)
2026-10-24 00:31:10 FINE  FdProjectionService - persistence context size = 0 (projection proxies not managed)
2026-10-24 00:31:10 INFO  FdProjectionService - [DTO] 3 rows, 3 columns (fd_id, principal, maturity_amount) — plain records
2026-10-24 00:31:10 INFO  FdProjectionService - [DYNAMIC] 2 rows returned as FdDto
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Client: GET /api/v1/fd-projections/summary/SAV2001
    │
    ▼
  FdProjectionController.summary("SAV2001")
    │
    ▼
  FdProjectionService (@Transactional readOnly=true)
    │ fdRepo.findByAccountId("SAV2001") : List<FdSummary>
    ▼
  Spring Data — closed interface projection
    │ SQL: SELECT f.fd_id, f.maturity_amount FROM fixed_deposits f WHERE f.account_id=?
    │ (10 other columns NOT read, incl. notes TEXT)
    ▼
  PostgreSQL ── 2 rows, 2 columns ──→ proxy objects (NOT in persistence context)
    │
    ▼
  Response: [{"fdId":"FD-001","maturityAmount":536250.00}, ...]

  ── THREE FORMS AT A GLANCE ──
  INTERFACE  → proxy over selected getters   → narrow SQL, small proxy overhead
  DTO/CLASS  → new FdDto(...) / record        → narrow SQL, no proxy, FASTEST
  DYNAMIC    → <T> findBy...(id, Class<T>)    → caller picks shape at runtime

  ── PERFORMANCE RANKING ──
  1. DTO/record  (fewest columns, no persistence context)
  2. Interface   (few columns, proxy layer)
  3. Full entity (all columns, snapshots, dirty checking)
```

```
  Interface = proxy over getters; DTO = JPQL "new" / record; dynamic = Class<T> arg.
  Projections read fewer columns and skip persistence-context tracking entirely.

  Observability: bytes scanned per query, projection vs entity latency. Security: minimal PII.
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
JPA projections let me fetch only the data a screen actually needs instead of hydrating a full entity, and Spring Data gives me three forms. The interface-based projection is a plain Java interface with getters that match entity properties; Spring Data builds a proxy and, for a closed projection, narrows the SQL to just those columns. The class or DTO projection uses a JPQL constructor expression like SELECT new FdDto with the parameters in the same order as the select clause, or a record return type that Spring Data maps automatically; this is the fastest form because the objects never enter the persistence context, so there is no proxy and no dirty-check snapshot. The dynamic projection declares a single finder with a generic type parameter and a Class argument, so the caller decides at runtime whether to get a lightweight interface, a DTO, or the full entity from one method.

In our fixed-deposit portal at National Bank of India, the summary list uses a closed interface projection that reads only the deposit id and maturity amount, which is two columns instead of twelve. The detail API uses a DTO constructor projection so the JSON contract is explicit and there are no lazy-proxy serialization surprises. The search screen uses a dynamic projection so the same query powers both a compact row and a full drill-down depending on a toggle, without duplicating finders.

The performance ordering I keep in mind is that the DTO projection is fastest because it reads the fewest columns and skips persistence-context management, the closed interface projection is close behind with a small proxy cost, and the full entity is slowest because every row carries a snapshot for dirty checking. The senior cautions are that an open interface projection using a SpEL expression must load the whole entity first and loses the column narrowing, and that nested interface projections across associations can quietly trigger an extra query per row, so I keep projections flat and move to a DTO whenever I need computed or joined values.
